title: The Raven and the Fox — Chapter Summary
intro: Aesop's classic fable about a hungry fox who flatters a vain raven into dropping a piece of cheese. The fable teaches a sharp lesson about flattery — when someone praises you a lot, ask yourself: what do they want?

overview_diagram.title: The Raven and the Fox — overview

branches.label: Moral
details: Beware of those who praise you

sections.heading: The Fable
bullets: A raven steals a piece of cheese and flies up to a tree branch.
A hungry fox sees the cheese but cannot climb up.
The fox flatters the raven — praises his black feathers and beautiful wings.
He asks the raven to sing, suggesting such a beautiful bird must have a wonderful voice.
The raven, full of pride, opens his beak to caw — the cheese falls.
The fox grabs the cheese, runs off, and tells the raven: 'voice but no SENSE'.

sections.heading: Vocabulary
bullets: flatter — to praise someone excessively, usually because you want something.
vain — too proud of one's appearance or qualities.
pride — feeling pleased with oneself; excessive self-importance.
cunning — clever in a sneaky way.
sense — good judgement; common sense.
beak — the hard pointed mouth of a bird.
branch — an arm-like part of a tree.

sections.heading: Comprehension
bullets: The fox's compliments are NOT sincere — they are a trick.
The fox exploits the raven's vanity — his weakness.
By asking the raven to sing, the fox forces him to open his beak.
The raven loses the cheese because he values being praised more than the food.
The closing words — 'voice but no SENSE' — drive home the lesson.

sections.heading: Language Focus
bullets: PRONOUNS replace nouns (he, she, it, they) — they avoid repetition.
DIRECT SPEECH uses quotation marks: The fox said, "What a beautiful raven you are!"
ADVERBS describe HOW / WHEN / WHERE an action is done — many end in -ly (quickly, sweetly, softly).
Aesop's poem uses RHYME — pairs of words that sound alike at the end (cheese / ease, fox / rocks, refuse / news).
ADJECTIVES still appear too: sly, hungry, beautiful, shining.

sections.heading: Apply the Moral
bullets: When someone praises you a lot, pause and ask: 'why are they saying this?'
Distinguish genuine appreciation from flattery — flattery has a hidden goal.
Pride is not bad in moderation, but EXCESSIVE pride blinds us.
The lesson applies in advertising, friendships, even social media.

key_takeaways: Aesop's fables are short stories with sharp morals.
The fox uses flattery to trick the raven into dropping the cheese.
The moral: beware of flatterers — they often want something from you.
Vocabulary: flatter, vain, pride, cunning, sense.
Pronouns replace nouns; direct speech uses quotation marks; adverbs often end in -ly.
Apply the moral in real life: when praised, ask 'what do they want?'
